citations.narrative:
Surfaces inside the primary enclosure for two non-human primates are not kept clean or in good repair:
**There is a soiled and damaged rope hammock in the outdoor side of the enclosure for one adult male bonnet macaque
named "Petey". The rope is frayed, broken in places and stained a brownish color.
**There is a plastic flap covered in a brown substance between the indoor and outdoor portions of the enclosure for one
adult male capuchin named "George". The facility representative states that it will not come off despite cleaning attempts.
Damaged enrichment can result in injury to non-human primates from entrapment or ingestion, and surfaces that cannot
be readily cleaned and sanitized can attract pests and vermin and harbor harmful bacteria that can harm the animals. The
facility must ensure that all surfaces are maintained on a regular basis and that objects within the facility are replaced
when worn or soiled to protect the animals from illness or injury.
TO BE CORRECTED BY 09/10/2026

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The premises in and around non-human primates are not kept clean and free of discarded materials:
**There is faded and crumpled trash pressed into the grass and hanging between the wires of the outdoor portions of the
primary enclosures holding three adult female lemurs and one adult male capuchin.
**There are accumulations of dirt/debris in numerous places on the floor inside the room containing 3 adult female lemurs
and one adult male capuchin. Uncontained trash and rubble piles, as well as dirty floors near animal enclosures can
harbor or attract microbes, pests and vermin that can cause illness or injury to the animals or contaminate food and food
prep areas.
The licensee must ensure that premises where housing facilities are located, including buildings and surrounding
grounds, are kept clean and in good repair in order to protect the nonhuman primates from injury, to facilitate the
husbandry practices required in this subpart, and to reduce or eliminate breeding and living areas for rodents, pests, and
vermin. Premises must be kept free of accumulations of trash, junk, waste, and discarded matter; weeds, grass, and
bushes must be controlled so as to facilitate cleaning of the premises and pest control.
TO BE CORRECTED BY 09/14/2026

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
Although there are rodent traps in several indoor areas, there is not an effective pest control program in place because
there are accumulations of rodent droppings in numerous places on the floor inside the food prep and storage areas and
the rooms containing four adult ring-tailed lemurs, one adult bonnet macaque and one adult male capuchin.
Rodents and their droppings can harbor parasites and other disease-causing agents that can harm the animals. An
effective program for control of insects, external parasites affecting nonhuman primates, and birds and mammals that are
pests, must be established and maintained so as to promote the health and well-being of the animals and reduce
contamination by pests in animal areas.

Food meant for the consumption of animals is stored improperly. Inside the area containing primary enclosures for three
adult bobcats, there are packages of thawed chicken pieces and lunch meat inside an open container, left outside on the
ground in partial sun with swarming flies. A facility representative stated that an employee must have gone to lunch and
left the food to be fed upon return. Another representative stated that employees go to lunch at 12pm, and the food was
found at 1:29pm during inspection.
Failure to properly store food can cause it to deteriorate or become contaminated, which can result in unpalatability,
decreased nutritive value and cause animal illness. The licensee must ensure that supplies of food and bedding are
stored in facilities which adequately protect such supplies against deterioration, molding, or contamination by vermin.
Refrigeration shall be provided for supplies of perishable food.
TO BE CORRECTED FROM THE DATE OF THIS INSPECTION ON 09/02/2026 AND GOING FORWARD

The facility does not have a perimeter fence of sufficient height and integrity where required on the premises. Portions of
the front fence line are constructed of brick and a wrought iron sliding gate; when the gate is closed and not overlapping
the brick wall portion, the wall is ~57-70" here and in some other sections that were recently replaced. This is short of the
required 72" height for the species maintained at the facility. The licensee made changes to the shorter fencing around
the areas housing 3 adult bobcats by attaching pieces of tree branches to it and stringing two strands of wire between the
branches along the fence, with exception of the parts of the fence that have gates, which are only 48" to 57" in height.
There are approximately 3 sections where the modified fencing with tree branches stops without adjoining to another
section of perimeter fence that is of sufficient height. The wire strung between the tree branches is sagging in some
places with gaps of about 8-12" between the wire strands; these strands are easily moved by one finger by the inspector.
The fence is inadequate because it may not serve as an effective, secondary containment system for all the animals
housed at the facility and may not prevent other animals and unauthorized people from entering where it is weak or of
insufficient height. The licensee must assess all perimeter fences at the facility for adequate height and structural integrity
and modify the existing fence(s) or install a different perimeter fence or fences of at least 72" in height. The perimeter
fence(s) must be a minimum of three feet from the primary enclosures and so cannot also serve as any of the walls of a
primary enclosure. The perimeter fence must be constructed so that it protects the animals by restricting entry of outside
animals and unauthorized persons from going through it, or under it, or having contact with the animals in the facility.
These criteria apply to all sections of fence that serve as a perimeter fence.
TO BE CORRECTED BY 09/23/2026

The kitchen and outdoor areas have accumulations of rubble, trash and/or food waste and other debris:
**There is a layer of dust and rodent feces with dried up food waste (a bone and other debris) around the refrigerator and
other parts of the kitchen area and an indoor animal housing room.
**There is an overturned, open trash can with garbage spilling out of it outside near outdoor animal housing areas, as well
as a stack of discarded pallets near the spilled can.
**There is weathered wood and old Halloween decorations in a heap on the ground inside the area containing the primary
enclosures for three adult bobcats.
**There is a desiccated bird carcass in the enclosure housing one adult bobcat; the facility representative did not know
when it was given to the bobcat or how long it had been there.
Accumulations of trash, food waste and unused materials can attract pests and vermin that can cause harm to the
animals. The licensee must ensure that premises (buildings and grounds) are kept clean and in good repair in order to
protect the animals from injury and illness, and to facilitate the prescribed husbandry practices set forth in Part 3, Subpart
F. Accumulations of trash shall be placed in designated areas and cleared as necessary to protect the health of the
animals.

Despite there being a few rodent traps seen in a nearby room, there are accumulations of mouse droppings, some of
which appear fresh, in numerous places on the floor around the refrigerator and other places in the kitchen area, as well
as in the room containing two adult kinkajous, one adult Virginia opossum, two prairie dogs and three adult chinchillas.
The facility representative explained that spray foam is used to help keep the rodents from entering the building along
walls and doors, and there is a line of this foam on the bottom edge of a door with a hole in a nearby room that opens up
to a shared hallway where small rodents can enter. Wild rodents can harbor or spread parasites and disease-causing
microbes that can contaminate food and food prep areas and cause injury or illness to the animals. The licensee must
establish and maintain a safe and effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian
pests so as to promote the health and well-being of the animals.
TO BE CORRECTED BY 09/14/2026
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives and the licensee.
